answers.name: the guided reading list
answers.unclear: Only that the order of the rows matters (it is a reading path), and the poster has no word for an ordered collection. Each row is one document, edited in place, and membership is chosen by hand.

answers.name: the tracker registry, a cache rebuilt from each tracker's tasks/
answers.unclear: Each entry shows status counts for its tasks but has no status of its own, so tracker does not apply. The poster does not say whether a rollup of statuses counts toward that word.

answers.name: the outpost observation stream
answers.unclear: Each row is a dated observation of one file (installed, verified or differs). Rows are appended and never rewritten, which is the stream. But the verified and differs rows are readings of a file's state, and snapshot is defined as 'a reading, kept as of its date'. Its 'checks readings' example is dated readings of files and their comparisons, which looks close to this. I chose stream because rows arrive one at a time as observations happen, while a snapshot is taken whole on one date. The poster does not draw that line, and one install report (an event) and one comparison (a reading) fall on opposite sides of it. The file currently holds only its header.

answers.collection: window.__traffic, the in-memory traffic ledger in web-tools lib/gh-boot.js
answers.name: the page's capped request record: live per-call rows, the oldest dropped past 400 (a 'window', if call 4 adopts it)
answers.unclear: Each entry is one fetch (an event). It is pushed with status 0 and ms 0, then rewritten when the call settles (status, ms, wire, rate, error) and again by __noteApiError, so the record changes until its event ends. The poster lists 'the traffic logs' under stream, but those are the files in web-tools-private logs/traffic/, not this array. A reader going by the name alone would put this in stream. The 400-row cap that drops the oldest entries is call 4, which the poster leaves open, and none of the four add-on words describes it.

answers.name: the sessions cache: summaries of the newest 400 session records
answers.unclear: Each row summarizes one session (an event) and is re-read whenever that session's record moves. The live session rewrites on every Stop, so this sits in the empty box, like the session records it is rebuilt from (hence cache). I added tracker because each row carries a 'state' (ready, pending, merged, done), the session's own closing claim. Whether a status the session reports about itself counts as 'a status, such as open or done' is my judgment. The 400-row cap (ROW_CAP) is again call 4, the 'window', which has no word. And the poster's empty box has no name to give this, so I could only describe it.

answers.name: dated source snapshots (single intakes and series of intakes)
answers.unclear: A single-intake bundle is a dated folder that is never revised, which matches 'a reading, kept as of its date'. A series bundle gains new intakes and its acquired date moves, so the series as one entry changes over time. That looks like a registry of snapshots, and the poster has no rule for a collection whose entries are themselves collections. The bundle and file tables the script writes would be caches, but they are not the bundles themselves.

answers.name: a cache of enacted budget decisions, 2019-2026 (a stream of line movements)
answers.unclear: Each row is one enacted line movement in one legislative session, an event that does not change, so stream. But nothing is added as things happen: build-decision-ledger.py rebuilds the whole file from one dated pull (the 2026-06-04 longitudinal bundle, itself a snapshot) plus authored driver rules, hence cache. The driver and persistence columns can change on a rebuild when the rules change. The poster does not say whether a derived table takes its box from its entries (events), from its upstream (a snapshot), or from how its columns behave on a rebuild (changes after written, which would point to registry).

answers.name: the errand request queue
answers.unclear: The poster names errands outright in call 3 ('not snapshots', recommended 'request queue') but leaves the call open, so no box on the grid is confirmed. That is why I answered none. By the grid itself the case is mixed: a request file never changes, an errand is open until a result file closes it, and a Gemini result 'gains later ones' until it is marked settled, so the errand's record is rewritten until its event ends. That is the empty box, and call 3's 'never change either' is not quite true. Tracker is my judgment: open, claimed and closed (completed or declined) are statuses, but they come from which files exist rather than a field on the entry. The errand records are on the background branch. I fetched that ref read-only to look, then deleted the local ref.

poster: Two parts worked. The two-question grid quickly sorted the clear cases: aims-reading as a hand-picked registry, trackers.md as a cached registry. The add-on words were easy to apply as yes/no checks. It was weakest where an entry is a dated reading but the collection grows a row at a time (observations.csv, source bundles). The thing/event split decides between snapshot and stream there, and the poster gives no test for whether a reading is a thing or an event. Its examples work against it in places: 'the traffic logs' under stream invites filing window.__traffic there by name, though its rows are rewritten until each call settles. Three of my eight answers ran into its own open calls: the empty box (traffic ledger, sessions cache), the cap or 'window' (both of those again), and the request queue (errands). For those I could only describe the collection, not name it. It also has no rule for derived tables whose rows are events (decision-ledger), or for collections of collections (series bundles).
